# Introduction
This notebook performs an exploratory data analysis (EDA) on lung cancer mortlity data in the United States, covering the years **2000 to 2019**.  
This data were downloaded from **https://ghdx.healthdata.org/record/ihme-data/us-lung-cancer-county-race-ethnicity-2000-2019**.
Our notebook explores patterns and disparities in lung cancer mortality across the United States from 2000 to 2019. We will begin by introducing the dataset and its key variables, then examine national trends on each variables, and finally investigate demographic and geographic disparities over time.

# Dataset and Motivation
Currently, there are more than 100 types of cancers around the world. Of all, lung cancer has been the first and most diagnosed cancer. It became a threat to public health worldwide. By 2020, there were nearly 2 million cases related to lung cancer deaths. (Tesfaw et al.). While screenings such as low-dose computed tomography can significantly reduce lung cancer mortality, access to these screenings remains unevenly distributed and often limited, especially for vulnerable populations. The barriers to screening include a lack of awareness about risk factors, financial constraints, and geographic limitations. Existing studies has shown that lung cancer is often correlated to comorbid conditions (e.g. hypertension, diabetes), and behavioral and environmental links. While disparities in cancer has been systematically studied, not many existing literature discussed how these disparities have shifted throughout time. 

This dataset includes the year of observation, state, sex, age group, race, and the mortality rate (deaths per 100,000 residents). By analyzing these variables together, we can track how lung cancer mortality has changed over time in the US, compare rates between men and women, examine differences among racial and age groups, and identify geographic patterns across states. This not only enable us to explore the national trends, but also disparities that may exist between different populations and regions.

With the variables in our current dataset, we aim to address the following questions:
1. How have lung cancer mortality rates changed nationally over the past two decades?
2. What disparities exist across sex, age, and race?
3. How have these disparities shifted over time?


# Package Set Up
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)
library(GGally)
```

# Forming our Dataset
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Combining all yearly CSV files together (all csv file have the exact same data structure, varied by year)
male_files <- list.files("data/male", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
female_files <- list.files("data/female", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)

male_data <- male_files %>%
  map_dfr(~ read_csv(.x) %>% clean_names()) %>%
  mutate(sex_name = "Male")

female_data <- female_files %>%
  map_dfr(~ read_csv(.x) %>% clean_names()) %>%
  mutate(sex_name = "Female")

lung_cancer_df <- bind_rows(male_data, female_data)
```

# Quick Overview

```{r}
glimpse(lung_cancer_df)
```
The raw dataset contains over 16 million rows and 19 columns, indicating a highly detailed breakdown by sex, race, age, and geography over time. Most columns like sex_name, race_name, age_name, and location_name will need cleaning or renaming for easier analysis. Additionally, the mortality rates are stored under val, with corresponding confidence intervals in lower and upper.

## Data Preprocessing
Before getting started on our analysis, we begin with data preprocessing to make sure our data is organized and cleaned. We normalized the mortality rate to better visualize this data when plotted. The state names were also extracted to form the new state varaible. In addition, msissing values are dropped from the dataset.
```{r}
# Clean and Structure Data
lung_clean <- lung_cancer_df %>%
  mutate(
    state = str_extract(location_name, "(?<=\\().+?(?=\\))"),
    state = if_else(is.na(state), location_name, state),
    
    # Normalize death rate per 100,000 population
    mortality_rate = val * 100000,
    lower_ci = lower * 100000,
    upper_ci = upper * 100000
  ) %>%
  select(
    year,
    state,
    sex = sex_name,
    age_group = age_name,
    race = race_name,
    mortality_rate,
    lower_ci,
    upper_ci
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(mortality_rate), state != "United States of America")

# Missing Values Check
colSums(is.na(lung_clean))
unique(lung_clean$state)
```


After cleaning, the new dataset contains approximately **9 million rows** and **8 columns**.
```{r}
# Preview of Cleaned Data
glimpse(lung_clean)
```


# National Trends Over Time
## 1. Overall Mortality Rate (2000–2019)

```{r}
nat_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(nat_trend, aes(x = year, y = mean_rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "National Lung Cancer Mortality Rate (2000–2019)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000 (Age-adjusted)"
  )
```

The national average lung cancer mortality rate decreased steadily from ~112 deaths per 100,000 in 2000 to ~82 deaths per 100,000 in 2019.  
This decline likely reflects reduced smoking prevalence, improved screening methods, and better treatments over the past two decades.

## 2. Mortality Trends By Sex
```{r}
sex_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarize(rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(sex_trend, aes(x = year, y = rate, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Lung Cancer Mortality by Sex (2000–2019)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000",
    color = "Sex"
  )


```
  
  Males have consistently higher mortality rates compared to females, with rates falling from ~150 to ~100 deaths per 100,000.Females saw a much slower decline, with their curve flattening between 2005 and 2010. This may suggest that tobacco cessation and health campaigns initially targeted men more effectively or that historical smoking rates among women lagged behind men.


## 3. Mortality Trends By Age Group
```{r}
age_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  group_by(year, age_group) %>%
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(age_trend, aes(x = year, y = mean_rate, color = age_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Lung Cancer Mortality by Age Group",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000",
    color = "Age Group"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")


```

Older groups show much higher mortality, exceeding 400 deaths per 100,000. Younger age groups (<50 years) maintain low and nearly flat rates, indicating that lung cancer remains predominantly an illness affecting older adults. The decline in older age groups suggests improvements in screening and treatment for seniors, as well as the cumulative effect of reduced smoking over time.

Kentucky, West Virginia, Maine ,and Mississippi are among the states with the highest mortality rates (>120 deaths per 100,000). Utah and Colorado show the lowest rates, likely due to lower smoking rates and stronger public health measures. The sharp contrast between states underscores the impact of local health policies and cultural habits.



```{r}

```

American Indian and Alaska Native groups have the highest lung cancer mortality rates, which increased between 2000 and 2005 before declining. Black populations started with the highest rate in 2000 but achieved significant reductions, approaching parity with other races by 2019. Asian populations show relatively stable, low mortality, possibly due to lower historical smoking prevalence.

After confirming the disparities in mortality rates, we want to further investigate how much mortality rate is affected by these observed factors and whether these relationships are significant, which we perform a regression analysis below.  

## Regression Analysis
```{r}

# Filter out unnecessary age groups for our model
lung_clean_filtered <- lung_clean %>%
  filter(!age_group %in% c(
    "<1 year", "1 to 4", "5 to 9", "10 to 14", "All Ages", 
    "Age-standardized"
  ))

# Convert predictors to factors since they are categorical
lung_clean_filtered$sex <- as.factor(lung_clean_filtered$sex)
lung_clean_filtered$race <- as.factor(lung_clean_filtered$race)
lung_clean_filtered$age_group <- as.factor(lung_clean_filtered$age_group)

# Explicitly setting the reference level since R will by default, choose its reference based on alphabetical order
lung_clean_filtered$age_group <- relevel(lung_clean_filtered$age_group, ref = "60 to 64")
lung_clean_filtered$sex <- relevel(lung_clean_filtered$sex, ref = "Male")
lung_clean_filtered$race <- relevel(lung_clean_filtered$race, ref = "White")
```

Here is our regression model with year, sex, race, and age group being the predictor variables, and mortality rate as response variable:
```{r}
model <- lm(mortality_rate ~ year + sex + race + age_group, data = lung_clean_filtered)

summary(model)
```
We achieved a R-squared of 0.75, which means that about 75% of the variability in mortality rate is explained by the model. All of our predictors are statistically significant (p < 0.001), meaning they all show a meaningful relationship with mortality rate. 

We also performed a regression model without year. We expect the coefficients of these variables to shift if the disparities have changed over time. 

```{r}
model_2 <- lm(mortality_rate ~ sex + race + age_group, data = lung_clean_filtered)

summary(model_2)
```
Here, we observe that the coefficients remained identical as Model 1 (with year). This means that the effects of sex, race, and age on lung cancer mortality are relatively stable over time. From this, we learned that the gap between males and females, or between races, is not narrowing or widening significantly from 2000 to 2019. This also indicates that year affects the overall mortality trend but not on the demographic gaps.

### Interpretation of Regression Result on Model 1
- Year: Each year, lung cancer mortality rate decreases by 2.19, holding all else constant.
- Female: Females have about 78 fewer deaths per 100,000 than males, holding all else constant.
- American Indian/Alaska Native: AIAN individuals have a 13.42 units higher mortality rate than white individuals.
- Asian: Asians have a 76.82 units lower mortality rate than white individuals.
- Black: Black individuals have a 9.87 units higher mortality rate than white individuals.
- Latino: Latino individuals have a 89.85 units lower mortality rate than white individuals.
- all younger age groups below our reference level of 60-64 shows lower mortality rate, while all older age groups above our reference level shows higher mortality rate.This aligns with expectations that lung cancer risk increases with age. 


Temporal Trend: 

Our model shows that mortality rates are declining over time, with approximately 2.19 reduction each year.

Sex Differences:  

Males continue to have a greater incidence of lung cancer compared to females, even when race, age group, and year are controlled. This observation aligns with the historical trends of lung cancer related to tobacco use; males have been more prone to smoking and occupational lung cancer risks.  

Racial Disparities:  

Latinos and Asians showed a significantly lower mortality rate compared to white individuals, whereas Blacks and AIAN groups have higher mortality rate compared to white individuals, holding all else constant.  

Age Effect:  

The pattern of the data confirms that the younger age group, controlling for other factors, contains the lowest mortality rates. On the other hand, the older age group shows higher mortality rates. This confirms the effect of a combination of biological factors and the long-term accumulation of risk factors in smoking.


## Conclusion

This exploratory data analysis has revealed several critical patterns and disparities in lung cancer mortality in the United States from 2000 to 2019. Using a comprehensive, age-adjusted dataset sourced from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), we examined trends across time, demographic subgroups, and geographic regions. The insights drawn from this analysis have substantial implications for public health research, policy development, and future intervention strategies.

### 1. National Mortality Trends

One of the most striking findings is the nationwide decline in lung cancer mortality over the past two decades. From approximately 112 deaths per 100,000 people in 2000, the age-adjusted national average dropped to around 82 deaths per 100,000 by 2019—a reduction of over 25%. This decline reflects the culmination of long-term public health initiatives, such as anti-smoking campaigns, policy reforms like indoor smoking bans, improved early detection through screening, and advancements in treatment technologies such as immunotherapy and targeted therapies.

However, while the national trend is encouraging, the decline has not been uniformly distributed across all population groups or geographic areas. This underscores the importance of disaggregating the data to uncover hidden inequities in progress.

### 2. Disparities by Sex and Age

When we stratify the mortality rates by sex, we find that men have consistently experienced significantly higher lung cancer mortality than women throughout the 20-year period. Male mortality began at over 150 deaths per 100,000 in 2000, decreasing to about 100 by 2019. In contrast, female mortality started lower and declined more gradually, with some stagnation observed between 2005 and 2010.

These sex-based differences are likely rooted in historical smoking behavior, as men adopted and abandoned smoking earlier than women. Additionally, early public health messaging often targeted men more aggressively, while female smoking rates rose later in the 20th century and may have plateaued at different times depending on social and cultural factors. The slower decline in female mortality could also point to gaps in screening or treatment access for women in specific age or socioeconomic groups.

In terms of age, older adults remain disproportionately affected. Individuals over 65 consistently showed the highest mortality rates, with some age groups exceeding 400 deaths per 100,000. Meanwhile, younger age groups (<50 years) exhibited much lower and relatively stable mortality trends. This reflects the latency period of lung cancer, which typically manifests after decades of exposure to risk factors like smoking or industrial pollutants. The improvements seen in older adults likely result from targeted screening programs such as low-dose CT scans and broader reductions in smoking among seniors.

### 3. Geographic Inequities

Our analysis also revealed stark geographic disparities in lung cancer mortality. States like Kentucky, West Virginia, and Mississippi consistently ranked among those with the highest rates—often exceeding 120 deaths per 100,000. These states are known for higher smoking prevalence, rural populations with limited access to healthcare, and socioeconomic challenges such as poverty and low education levels, all of which contribute to worse health outcomes.

On the other end of the spectrum, states like Utah and Colorado demonstrated some of the lowest mortality rates. These regions benefit from strong public health systems, robust anti-smoking legislation, and generally healthier lifestyles. The geographic contrast suggests that state-level policy, economic conditions, and healthcare infrastructure play a substantial role in determining lung cancer outcomes.

### 4. Racial and Ethnic Trends

Racial disparities in lung cancer mortality present another crucial dimension. Our analysis found that the American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) populations experienced the highest mortality rates across the study period. Their rates rose initially between 2000 and 2005 and then gradually declined, but they remained the most impacted racial group from 2005 onward. This trend may reflect historical underinvestment in Native health services, higher smoking rates, and limited access to preventive care.

Black Americans, who started with the highest mortality rate in 2000, showed one of the most dramatic improvements over the study period, approaching parity with other groups by 2019. This progress suggests that interventions targeting smoking cessation and lung health within Black communities may have begun to take effect. In contrast, Asian Americans consistently had the lowest mortality rates, which remained stable with only minor variation. This could be attributed to lower smoking prevalence and possibly genetic or environmental factors that warrant further investigation.

While the general downward trend in all racial groups is a positive sign, the persistence of gaps between groups is a reminder that one-size-fits-all public health solutions are insufficient. Culturally tailored outreach, healthcare access expansion, and community-based interventions remain vital for addressing these inequities.

### Final Reflections

This exploratory project emphasizes the value of data disaggregation and visualization in identifying invisible disparities. While the overarching trend is one of improvement, the differences by sex, age, race, and location show that progress has not been uniform. In many ways, these findings mirror larger systemic issues in American healthcare, where demographic and regional factors heavily influence outcomes.

Looking forward, our results suggest a few key areas for future attention:

- Continued investment in tobacco prevention and cessation, particularly in high-risk populations and high-mortality states.
- Targeted screening and early detection programs for seniors and underserved racial groups.
- Policy support for equitable healthcare access, especially in rural and economically disadvantaged communities.

By combining high-quality data with rigorous analysis, we can guide better decision-making and ultimately contribute to reducing the burden of preventable deaths from lung cancer across all populations in the United States.
